diagrams.name: mat-p414-mechanics
diagrams.title: Basic concepts in mechanics: forces and properties

diagrams.name: mat-p415-microleakage
diagrams.title: Consequences of microleakage at the restoration margin

cloze.text: Normal masticatory force on molars is about {{c1::90–200}} pounds — and much more on the cusp tips.
{{c1::Tensile}} force pulls objects apart and elongates them (e.g., pulling a rope from opposing sides).
{{c1::Compressive}} force puts pressure on an object (e.g., heavy lifting, CPR chest compressions).
{{c1::Shear}} force pushes one part of an object in one direction and another part in the opposite direction, with a twisting or rotating motion (e.g., the two handles of scissors acting on the pin).
{{c1::Stress}} is the internal force that resists an applied force; it can resist the external force up to the point of {{c2::fracture}}.
The {{c1::larger}} the area over which stress acts, the more distributed the stress (e.g., flat running shoes put less stress on the foot than heels).
{{c1::Amalgam}} and {{c1::composite}} have stress-bearing ability similar to natural tooth {{c2::enamel}}.
{{c1::Ductility}} is the ability to withstand deformation under stress before fracturing or breaking.
{{c1::Brittleness}} is the tendency to fracture or break before deformation occurs.
{{c1::Malleability}} is the ability to be compressed without fracturing.
{{c1::Strain}} is the deformation of a material in response to stress — a change in size and shape.
{{c1::Elasticity}} is the ability of an object to return to its original shape when the load is removed.
The {{c1::modulus of elasticity}} measures the {{c2::stiffness}} of an elastic material (e.g., wires or rods being stretched or compressed).
cloze.extra: Stiffness matters when selecting restorative materials — they must withstand the forces of mastication.

cloze.text: The oral environment is wet, {{c1::acidic}}, and the {{c2::salts}} of saliva facilitate the movement of electrical current among metals.
{{c1::Galvanism}} is a direct current of electricity, especially when produced by chemical action; it causes {{c2::galvanic shock}}.
Everyday activities such as {{c1::drinking, eating, and smoking}} change the temperature in the oral cavity, which may cause changes in dental restorations over time.
{{c1::Thermal conductivity}} is the ability of heat to spread.
Metals are {{c1::excellent}} thermal conductors; cements and varnish are {{c2::poor}} thermal conductors.
cloze.extra: That is why cements/varnish are placed on the pulpal side of deep cavity preparations before metal restorations.

cloze.text: The {{c1::coefficient of thermal expansion}} is the change in volume and length of an object in response to a change in temperature.
The {{c1::higher}} the coefficient of thermal expansion, the greater the degree of contraction and expansion.
Ideally, a restorative material's coefficient of thermal expansion should be {{c1::closest to that of the natural tooth}}.
A difference in thermal expansion coefficient between tooth and material can cause {{c1::microleakage}} and {{c2::percolation}}.
{{c1::Microleakage}} is leakage of fluid and bacteria at the interface of the tooth and the restoration margins, caused by microscopic gaps.
Microleakage allows penetration of saliva, biofilm and by-products, which can lead to {{c1::secondary caries}}, pulpitis, pain, and necrosis.

{{c1::Percolation}} is the movement of fluid in the microscopic gap at the restoration margin caused by differing expansion/contraction rates of tooth and restoration with {{c2::temperature changes}}.
{{c1::Retention}} is the ability of a material to maintain position without being displaced under stress.
In {{c1::mechanical bonding}}, the material penetrates irregularities (pores in tooth structure) and interlocks mechanically.
cloze.extra: Example: acid etch creates pores for sealant material to flow into and attach.

cloze.text: {{c1::Wetting}} is the degree to which a liquid adhesive spreads over a surface; the better the spread, the {{c2::more}} retention.
In poor wetting the liquid beads up and the contact angle is {{c1::above::above/below}} 90° (e.g., liquid on a Teflon pan); in good wetting the liquid spreads (angle below 90°).
{{c1::Viscosity}} is a liquid material's ability to flow: {{c2::high}}-viscosity materials are thicker and do not flow well.
{{c1::Cohesion}} is attraction between {{c2::like}} atoms and molecules within a material, resulting in a tenacious bond (e.g., water molecule to water molecule).
{{c1::Adhesion}} is attraction between {{c2::unlike}} atoms and molecules on two different surfaces in contact (e.g., water molecule to a tree leaf).
The {{c1::larger}} the contact area, the better the chance of adhesion; bonding in dentistry is a type of {{c2::adhesion}}.
For a dental material to be aesthetically acceptable, it is important to understand how our {{c1::eyes sense colors}}.
{{c1::Hue}} is the color itself (e.g., blue, green, yellow); all hues can theoretically be mixed from the light primaries {{c2::red, green, and blue}}.
{{c1::Chroma}} is the intensity or strength of a color.
{{c1::Value}} is the lightness or darkness of a color.
{{c1::Opaque}} materials absorb or block light (e.g., gold, amalgam).
{{c1::Transparent}} materials are see-through (e.g., clear aligners).
{{c1::Translucent}} materials are partially see-through (e.g., porcelain, resin composites, enamel, ceramic veneers).
{{c1::Hardness}} is a measure of resistance to {{c2::indentation}} when a compressive force is applied.
cloze.extra: Dental materials should be hard enough to withstand biting forces.

cloze.text: {{c1::Mohs}} scale of hardness compares minerals by their relative ability to {{c2::scratch}} another mineral.
On the Mohs scale, the hardest mineral is {{c1::diamond}} (10) and the softest is {{c2::talc}} (1).
{{c1::Knoop}} hardness examines the indentation made by a {{c2::diamond point}}, viewed under a microscope.
Impressions produce a {{c1::negative}} reproduction of the mouth.
Agar is a {{c1::reversible}} hydrocolloid; alginate is an {{c2::irreversible}} hydrocolloid.
Elastomeric impression materials include {{c1::polysulfide}}, {{c2::silicone}}, {{c3::polyether}}, and {{c4::vinyl polysiloxane (PVS)}}.
Agar and alginate are {{c1::hydrophilic}}; elastomeric materials are {{c2::hydrophobic}}.
cloze.extra: As printed in the book's table (it groups all elastomers together).

cloze.text: Agar's working mechanism: {{c1::heat}} turns it to a sol (liquid), and {{c2::cooling}} returns it to a gel — the sol ⇄ gel change is reversible.
Alginate sets by {{c1::chemical setting only}}, which cannot be reversed.
Elastomeric materials set by {{c1::chemical or light-cured}} setting, depending on the material type.
Detail accuracy: alginate is {{c1::less}} accurate than agar or elastomers; elastomers give {{c2::very high}} detail for precision restorations.
Agar's common use (per the book): {{c1::study models}}, with reusable trays; it needs a {{c2::water bath}} setup and special conditioning equipment, and is good for moisture.
cloze.extra: More technique-sensitive and less commonly used today.

cloze.text: {{c1::Alginate}} is used for preliminary impressions and study models; it is economical, quick, uses standard trays, and is the impression material most commonly used in {{c2::hygiene}}.
{{c1::Elastomeric}} impression materials are used for final impressions for crowns, bridges, inlays, onlays and implants.
Elastomers are rigid and dimensionally stable: {{c1::polyether}} is stiff, {{c2::vinyl (PVS)}} is stable and accurate.
Elastomers often require a {{c1::custom tray}}, especially polysulfide and polyether; they are more expensive but essential for high-precision restorations.
Before mixing alginate, {{c1::fluff}} the powder, then measure the appropriate amounts of water and powder.
Alginate: add the {{c1::powder to the water}}, stir for {{c2::60}} seconds and remove bubbles.
Load alginate on the tray with a spatula, starting from the {{c1::back}}, then smooth the surface with a {{c2::moistened finger}}.
Pull the patient's {{c1::lips and cheeks}} out, seat the tray, and hold it in place until the alginate sets.
Alginate water/powder ratio affects setting time: {{c1::thinner}} mixes need {{c2::more}} time.
The {{c1::higher}} the water temperature, the {{c2::faster}} alginate sets.
Break the seal of the tray and snap it out {{c1::quickly}} for less distortion.

To disinfect an alginate impression: rinse under water to remove saliva and blood, {{c1::spray with disinfectant}}, and place in a {{c2::sealed plastic bag}} for the time recommended by the manufacturer.
Pour the impression as soon as possible to prevent {{c1::syneresis}}.
{{c1::Syneresis}} is loss of water, mostly by {{c2::evaporation}}.
The opposite of syneresis is {{c1::imbibition}}, the ability to {{c2::absorb}} water.
{{c1::Mixing time}} is the time from the beginning to the completion of the mixing action.
{{c1::Working time}} is the time from the beginning of mixing to {{c2::initial setting}}.
{{c1::Initial setting time}} is the point when the material starts to harden and can no longer be changed.
{{c1::Final setting time}} is the point when the material is completely set and indentations can no longer be made.
A replica produces a {{c1::positive}} reproduction and is often called a cast or a model.
Naturally occurring gypsum is a white powdery mineral: calcium sulfate {{c1::dihydrate}} (CaSO₄·2H₂O).
Dental gypsum products are calcium sulfate {{c1::hemihydrate}}, obtained by a water-evaporation process called {{c2::calcination}}.
{{c1::Gypsum}} is the most commonly used material for replication in dentistry.
Mixing hemihydrate with water is an {{c1::exothermic}} reaction (it produces heat).
{{c1::Potassium sulfate}} is the accelerator for gypsum, reducing setting time by 5–10 minutes; {{c2::borax}} is a retarder that increases setting time.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "sulfate" → "fast fate" (speeds up); "borax" sounds like "brake" (slows down).

cloze.text: A gypsum cast usually requires about {{c1::one hour}} to set, but {{c2::warm}} water can accelerate setting.
All gypsum materials {{c1::expand}} upon setting (setting expansion).
{{c1::Wet strength}} is gypsum's strength when excess water is present; {{c2::dry strength}} is its strength when excess water is removed.
Model plaster is Type {{c1::II}}, dental stone is Type {{c2::III}}, and die stone is Type {{c3::IV and V}}.
Particle type: plaster is {{c1::irregular and porous}}; stone is less irregular; die stone is {{c2::non-porous, dense, smooth}}.
From plaster → stone → die stone, setting expansion {{c1::decreases}} and compressive strength {{c2::increases}}.
cloze.extra: Plaster: high expansion, low strength. Stone: low, moderate. Die stone: very low, highest.

cloze.text: {{c1::Plaster}} needs the most water, stone less, and {{c2::die stone}} the least water.
Gypsum colors: plaster is {{c1::white}}, stone is {{c2::yellow or white}}, die stone is {{c3::pink, blue, or green}}.
Plaster is used for diagnostic casts, study models, and {{c1::articulating}} models; stone for study and {{c2::denture}} models; die stone for {{c3::crowns and bridges}}.
{{c1::Plaster}} is the least expensive gypsum product and {{c2::die stone}} the most expensive.
Type {{c1::I}} gypsum is {{c2::impression plaster}}; it is no longer used because it is too rigid and breaks easily.
When mixing gypsum, add the {{c1::powder to the water}}.
Stir gypsum vigorously for {{c1::30–60}} seconds with a {{c2::metal}} spatula until the mix is glossy and smooth.
Before pouring, {{c1::dry}} the surface of the impression; pour gypsum into {{c2::one corner}} and gently vibrate to fill it in increments.
After the replica dries, trim the base of the model {{c1::perpendicular to the midline}}.
A {{c1::direct}} restoration is placed directly into the prepared tooth in one visit (e.g., a composite filling hardened with a curing light).
An {{c1::indirect}} restoration is made outside the mouth (usually in a lab) and placed later; it takes at least {{c2::two}} appointments.
cloze.extra: Example: crown — visit 1 prep + impression; lab makes crown; visit 2 cement.

cloze.text: A {{c1::crown}} covers the entire chewing surface of a tooth.
An {{c1::inlay}} fits within the cusps (used on molars/premolars).
An {{c1::onlay}} extends over one or more cusps and is larger than an inlay.
A {{c1::veneer}} is a thin shell bonded to the {{c2::facial}} surface of {{c3::anterior}} teeth for cosmetic improvement.
Gold resists {{c1::tarnishing}} (discoloration due to oxidation) and {{c2::corrosion}} (rust).
cloze.extra: It is also highly resistant to fracture and durable.

cloze.text: Gold may cause {{c1::galvanic shock}} (interaction between metals causing an electric current).
Gold's thermal expansion is the {{c1::closest}} to natural tooth structure.
PFM combines a {{c1::metal substructure}} with an outer layer of {{c2::porcelain}} for strength and cosmetics.
PFM restorations are {{c1::stronger}} than all-porcelain restorations because of the metal base.
In PFM restorations, the porcelain layer can {{c1::chip or fracture}} under heavy force or bruxism.
Over time a PFM crown can show a {{c1::dark metal line}} near the gingiva, especially if {{c2::gingival recession}} occurs.
PFM is commonly used for crowns and bridges, especially in {{c1::posterior}} teeth where strength is important.
Porcelain is a type of {{c1::ceramic}} with improved properties; it is strong and durable.
Porcelain is used to produce {{c1::dentures}}, PFM crowns, bridges, veneers, onlays and inlays.
Porcelain gives an excellent match to natural tooth color, intensity and translucency, and can {{c1::transmit light}}, giving a natural, vital appearance.
For patients with porcelain restorations, use {{c1::neutral sodium}} fluoride, not {{c2::acidulated}} fluoride, which may damage the restoration.
{{c1::Zirconia}} is a strong, tooth-colored ceramic used for crowns, bridges, and {{c2::implant abutments}}.
Zirconia is more {{c1::durable}} than porcelain and highly resistant to fracture.
Zirconia appears {{c1::radiopaque}} on radiographs.
Zirconia is {{c1::less}} translucent than traditional porcelain but {{c2::more}} aesthetic than metal-based restorations.
Composite is used in many types of restorations (e.g., dentures, mouth guards, {{c1::crowns}}).
The major component of composite is the organic resin matrix, {{c1::dimethacrylate (bis-GMA)}}; {{c2::silica}} is the filler.
cloze.extra: Book also says "dimethylglyoxime" is added for flowability (as printed).

cloze.text: Composite needs {{c1::polymerization}}, a chemical reaction converting individual monomer molecules into long polymer molecules.
{{c1::Polymerization shrinkage}} is contraction during the polymerization reaction and can cause {{c2::marginal leakage}}.
{{c1::Cross-linking}} is the chemical reaction that ties polymer molecules together.
Composite can be {{c1::light-cured}} or {{c1::self-cured}}.
Composite attaches to the tooth surface by {{c1::mechanical interlocking}} into enamel rods.
Composite is a {{c1::poor}} conductor of heat and electricity, so it insulates the dental pulp.
Composite has good {{c1::flow}}, making it easy to use, and is resistant to wear and fracture.
For patients with composite restorations, use neutral sodium fluoride, not {{c1::acidulated}} fluoride, which may damage the restoration.
Amalgam is an alloy of {{c1::mercury}} with various metals (silver, copper, tin, and zinc); an {{c2::alloy}} is a combination of two or more metals.
High-copper amalgam contains {{c1::40–60}}% silver, {{c2::27–30}}% tin, {{c3::13–30}}% copper, and 1% zinc, set with mercury.
In amalgam, {{c1::silver}} enables setting expansion and increases strength and corrosion resistance.
In amalgam, {{c1::copper}} increases strength and minimizes corrosion, tarnish, creep, and sensitivity; high-copper amalgams show fewer {{c2::marginal failures}} than low-copper ones.
In amalgam, {{c1::tin}} may cause setting contraction.
In amalgam, {{c1::zinc}} reduces oxidation of the other metals; zinc-containing amalgams last longer than non-zinc amalgams.
Amalgam is strong, especially in {{c1::compression}}, with compressive strength similar to {{c2::enamel}}, and is relatively inexpensive.
Amalgam has {{c1::lower}} tensile and shear strength, so it requires {{c2::bulk}} to resist breakage.
{{c1::Corrosion}} of amalgam is a chemical reaction with saliva or food.
cloze.extra: Book adds: "resulting in high thermal conductivity" (as printed).

cloze.text: {{c1::Creep}} is dimensional change of amalgam over time from {{c2::compression}}.
In amalgam, {{c1::galvanism}} is the conduction of electricity by metals in an acidic environment.
An {{c1::overhang}} can result if material is applied inaccurately, the matrix band is placed incorrectly, or the margin is polished inaccurately — relevant to all restorative materials.
{{c1::Trituration}} is the mechanical mixing of alloy and mercury; it takes {{c2::6–20}} seconds (follow the manufacturer's instructions).
Correctly triturated amalgam looks {{c1::shiny}} and is {{c2::cohesive}}.
{{c1::Undertrituration}} makes amalgam dull and crumbly; it hardens too quickly and fractures.
Lab ceramic restorations are usually made with porcelain or castable glass called {{c1::Dicor}}.
Ceramic restorations can be made chairside using {{c1::CEREC}} computerized design.
For inlays, ceramic is more {{c1::durable}} than composite.

Materials such as amalgam should {{c1::not}} be placed directly on tooth structure; cements/liners/bases/varnishes {{c2::protect}} the tooth, give thermal insulation near the pulp, and improve retention.
Depending on how it is mixed, the same material can serve as a {{c1::luting agent}}, a {{c2::base}}, or a {{c3::temporary restoration}}.
{{c1::Cements}} retain restorations in the mouth.

basic.back: Anything that can alter the state of an object
basic.extra: Board Alert (book): don't over-memorize these definitions — focus on the clinical applications (e.g., fluoride, air-polishing powders).

basic.front: Why are insulating bases placed under a deep amalgam restoration?
basic.back: Amalgam has high thermal conductivity — placed near the pulp it transmits heat/cold and causes pain

basic.front: How can grinding and clenching cause microleakage?
basic.back: The constant pressure creates tiny stress fractures between the tooth and the filling, letting in fluids and bacteria over time
basic.extra: Did you know (book): bruxism doesn't just wear down restorations.

basic.front: An alginate impression can't be poured right away. How should it be stored?
basic.back: Wrap it in a moist paper towel or keep it in high humidity (to prevent syneresis)
A replica of multiple teeth and surrounding soft tissues, used for study or diagnosis
A replica of a single tooth, used in the lab to fabricate crowns or other precise restorations

basic.front: What happens if a gypsum mix is vibrated for too long?
basic.back: More air bubbles form and the cast becomes weak

basic.front: Why isn't replacing a stable old amalgam with composite (for looks alone) always a good idea?
basic.back: It removes healthy tooth structure and may release more mercury during removal than leaving it in place
basic.extra: Did you know (book): unless there's a fracture, recurrent decay, or allergy, most experts recommend leaving it alone.

mcq.question: A material that breaks with little or no deformation when stressed is best described as:
mcq.explanation: Brittleness = fracture before deformation occurs. Ductility is the opposite — the material withstands deformation before it breaks.

mcq.question: A patient with a new metal restoration reports a sharp, brief jolt of pain whenever her fork touches the tooth. The most likely cause is:
mcq.explanation: Two metals (fork + restoration) in wet, acidic, salty saliva create a direct electrical current — galvanism. Percolation/microleakage cause sensitivity via fluid in marginal gaps, not an instant jolt on metal contact.

mcq.question: Which restorative material property best limits microleakage caused by temperature changes in the mouth?
options: A. A high coefficient of thermal expansion
C. A coefficient of thermal expansion close to that of tooth structure
mcq.answer: C. A coefficient of thermal expansion close to that of tooth structure
mcq.explanation: When tooth and restoration expand and contract at different rates, marginal gaps open (percolation/microleakage). Matching the tooth's coefficient (11.4) minimizes this; a high coefficient (e.g., resin 35) worsens it.

mcq.question: A sealant is placed on an occlusal surface that was not etched. The sealant beads up instead of flowing into the fissures. Which property is poor?
mcq.explanation: Beading (contact angle > 90°) = poor wetting, so less retention. Acid etching creates pores that let the sealant flow in and lock on mechanically.

mcq.question: Which statement about hardness testing is correct?
options: A. Mohs hardness is measured by indentation from a diamond point
B. Knoop hardness measures indentation from a diamond point under a microscope
C. On the Mohs scale, tooth enamel is 8
D. Talc is the hardest mineral on the Mohs scale
mcq.answer: B. Knoop hardness measures indentation from a diamond point under a microscope
mcq.explanation: Knoop = diamond-point indentation, read microscopically. Mohs ranks scratch resistance (diamond 10 … talc 1); enamel is 5 (topaz is 8).

mcq.question: A dentist needs a final impression for a three-unit bridge with the highest detail and dimensional stability. Which material is most appropriate?
mcq.explanation: Elastomers (PVS = stable and accurate) give very high detail for precision restorations. Alginate is less accurate and is used for preliminary impressions and study models.

mcq.question: An alginate impression is left on the counter for two hours before pouring. The resulting cast is inaccurate mainly because of:
mcq.explanation: Syneresis = water loss (mostly evaporation) that shrinks/distorts the alginate. Imbibition is the opposite — absorbing water (e.g., storing it soaking wet).

mcq.question: Which gypsum product should be used to fabricate a die for a crown?
mcq.explanation: Die stone is non-porous, dense and smooth, with very low setting expansion and the highest compressive strength — needed for precise crowns and bridges. Type III stone is for study and denture models.

mcq.question: A restoration fabricated in the lab that replaces one cusp of a molar but does not cover the entire occlusal surface is a(n):
mcq.explanation: An onlay extends over one or more cusps. An inlay stays within the cusps; a crown covers the entire chewing surface.

mcq.question: A patient has several anterior composite and porcelain restorations. Which in-office fluoride is most appropriate?
options: C. Any fluoride; restorations are unaffected
mcq.explanation: Acidulated fluoride may damage (etch) porcelain and composite restorations; neutral sodium fluoride is safe. Fluoride is still indicated.

mcq.question: An amalgam mix comes out of the triturator dull and crumbly. What is the most likely cause, and the consequence?
options: A. Overtrituration; it sets too slowly
B. Undertrituration; it hardens too quickly and fractures
C. Too much zinc; excessive expansion
D. Too much tin; galvanic shock
mcq.answer: B. Undertrituration; it hardens too quickly and fractures
mcq.explanation: A correct mix is shiny and cohesive; undertriturated amalgam is dull and crumbly, hardens too fast and fractures.
